opus-5.5.text:
I think in AI, ideas are actually pretty cheap. If you go to any conference or read through arXiv, you'll find that almost every reasonable idea has been proposed by someone, often many times. "Let the model think step by step," "let the model use tools," "let the model learn from feedback": these sound obvious once you say them. What separates something that changes the field from something that's just a line in a paper is whether you actually made it work.

And making it work is where all the real knowledge is. When you implement something, you hit a hundred small problems that nobody talks about: the data is messy, the evaluation is wrong, the model learns a shortcut you didn't expect, the training is unstable. Each of those problems teaches you something about how these systems really behave. That kind of understanding you can't get by thinking in the abstract. Often the idea you end up with after implementation is quite different from, and much better than, the idea you started with.

There's also something specific about this era of AI. It's very empirical. Our theoretical understanding lags far behind what the systems can do. In physics or math, a beautiful idea can carry a lot of weight by itself. In AI right now, intuition is often wrong, and the only reliable judge is the experiment. So I'd rather have a slightly crude idea that runs than an elegant one that only lives on a slide.

Finally, I think implementation keeps you honest. It's easy to talk about AGI, agents, the future, and sound smart. But when you have to build the thing, you're forced to confront what's actually hard. For me, that's where the fun is, and also where the progress comes from.

r001.rationale: The response says AI ideas are cheap and that many sound obvious once stated.

r002.rationale: It describes practical implementation problems, but does not identify breaking ideas into small, achievable steps as a central difficulty.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that in AI right now, ideas are cheap and almost everyone has the same ones. If you sit in any group meeting at Princeton or at OpenAI, or scroll through Twitter for ten minutes, you'll hear "we should let the model use tools," "we should let it reflect on its mistakes," "we should train on environments instead of static data." These are not secrets. The paper that gets remembered is the one where someone actually sat down and made it work, and discovered all the things that were wrong with the idea along the way.

That second part is really the point for me. When I was working on ReAct, the idea itself was almost embarrassingly simple: interleave reasoning and acting. You can say it in one sentence. But you don't understand the idea until you implement it. You find out that the prompt format matters more than you'd like, that the model gets stuck in loops in ways you didn't predict, that the environment you thought was easy, like a text game or a Wikipedia search, is actually where all the hard problems hide. The implementation is where the idea gets corrected. If I had only talked about it, I would still believe a version of it that's wrong.

There's also a selection effect in how people learn. I came from a physics background originally, and in physics there's a long tradition of theory being enough: you write down the equation, and the experiment comes later. Deep learning hasn't earned that yet. Our theories are mostly post-hoc stories about things that already worked. So if you want to actually know something, instead of believing something, you have to build it and watch what happens. The model is the experiment, and the experiment surprises you constantly.

And honestly, there's a personal reason. Talking about ideas feels productive, and it's seductive, especially when people start listening to you. You go to a panel, you say something that sounds deep about agents, people nod. But I notice that my best thinking happened when I was debugging a tree search that wouldn't converge, or watching an agent fail at the same web task for the fortieth time. Those moments force you to be concrete. The abstract conversation lets you stay vague, and vagueness is where bad ideas survive. So I try to keep a rule for myself: if I've been talking about something for more than a couple of weeks and haven't written any code, I'm probably fooling myself.

r001.rationale: The response says AI ideas are cheap, nearly everyone has the same ones, and they are not secrets, tying recognition to making them work.

r002.rationale: It describes implementation challenges such as prompt formats, loops, and environments, but does not identify breaking ideas into small, achievable steps as a central difficulty.

astra-6.text:
I think implementation forces you to be precise. It’s easy to say, “An AI system should be able to reason, plan, and learn from feedback.” But once you try to build it, you have to answer concrete questions: What information does it receive? What actions can it take? How do you know whether it succeeded? Those details often turn out to be the real research problem.

I don’t think ideas are unimportant. Building is a way of testing your ideas—and discovering better ones. If something fails, you can investigate why. If it works, other people can reproduce it and improve it. That gives the discussion a foundation beyond whether an argument sounds convincing.

So I value implementation because it closes the loop between what we think should work and what actually works. Especially in AI, that gap can be surprisingly large.

r001.rationale: The response says ideas are important and implementation tests them; it does not attribute low value to many ideas being obvious.

r002.rationale: It discusses answering concrete design questions, but does not identify breaking ideas into small, achievable steps as a central implementation difficulty.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s because an idea can sound convincing while leaving the hardest questions unanswered. Once you try to implement it, you have to be precise: What does the model actually see? What can it do? How do you know whether it worked? That’s where you discover whether your intuition was right.

In AI, there are so many plausible ideas that having one isn’t necessarily the bottleneck. The harder part is turning it into something you can test, learning from the failures, and improving it. Even a small experiment can move a discussion forward more than a long debate, because now you have something concrete to examine.

I still think talking about ideas is valuable. But I want that conversation to lead to an experiment. Implementation is how you make your thinking accountable to reality.

r001.rationale: The response says many AI ideas are plausible and that having an idea is not the bottleneck, but it does not say they have low value because they are obvious.

r002.rationale: It emphasizes testing ideas through experiments, but does not identify breaking implementation into small, achievable steps as a central difficulty.
